# $\chi^2$ test {.section}

Relation between categorical variables

## $\chi^2$ test {.smaller}

A "chi-squared test", also written as $\chi^2$ test, is any statistical hypothesis test wherein the sampling distribution of the test statistic is a chi-squared distribution when the null hypothesis is true. Without other qualification, 'chi-squared test' often is used as short for Pearson's chi-squared test.

Chi-squared tests are often constructed from a Lack-of-fit sum of squared errors. A chi-squared test can be used to attempt rejection of the null hypothesis that the data are independent.

Source: [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chi-squared_test)

## $\chi^2$ test statistic {.subsection}

$\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(\text{observed}_{ij} - \text{prediction}_{ij})^2}{\text{prediction}_{ij}}$

### Contingency table {.smalller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column style="transform: scale(.7);"}

$\text{observed}_{ij} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
o_{11} & o_{12} & \cdots & o_{1j} \\
o_{21} & o_{22} & \cdots & o_{2j} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
o_{i1} & o_{i2} & \cdots & o_{ij} 
\end{pmatrix}$

:::

::: {.column style="transform: scale(.7);"}

$\text{prediction}_{ij} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
p_{11}  & p_{12} & \cdots & p_{1j} \\
p_{21}  & p_{22} & \cdots & p_{2j} \\
\vdots  & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
p_{i1}  & p_{i2} & \cdots & p_{ij} 
\end{pmatrix}$

:::

:::

## $\chi^2$ distribution {.smaller .subsection}

The $\chi^2$ distribution describes the test statistic under the assumption of $H_0$, given the degrees of freedom. 

$df = (r - 1) (c - 1)$ where $r$ is the number of rows and $c$ the number of columns.

```{r chisq-distribution, echo=FALSE,render=TRUE}
#| output-location: slide

chi <- seq(0,8,.01)
df  <- c(1,2,3,6,8,10)
mycols <-  palette.colors(n = 7, palette = "Okabe-Ito")

plot( chi, dchisq(chi, df[1]), lwd = 2, col = mycols[1], type="l",
      main = "Chi squared distributions",
      ylab = "Density",
      ylim = c(0,1),
      xlab = "Chi squared")

lines(chi, dchisq(chi, df[2]), lwd = 2, col = mycols[2], type="l")
lines(chi, dchisq(chi, df[3]), lwd = 2, col = mycols[3], type="l")
lines(chi, dchisq(chi, df[4]), lwd = 2, col = mycols[4], type="l")
lines(chi, dchisq(chi, df[5]), lwd = 2, col = mycols[5], type="l")
lines(chi, dchisq(chi, df[6]), lwd = 2, col = mycols[6], type="l")

legend("topright", legend = paste("k =",df), col = mycols, lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

## Assumptions {.subsection .smaller}

* Independence
  * Each person contributes to one cell only (no repeated measures)
* Expected frequencies not too small
* No normality assumption (categorical variables are not continuous)

## Calculating $\chi^2$ {.subsection}

```{r chisq-observed-table, echo=TRUE}
observed <- table(results[, c("Lecture", "Personality")])
observed
```

$\text{observed}_{ij} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
`r observed[1,1]` & `r observed[1,2]` \\
`r observed[2,1]` & `r observed[2,2]` \\
\end{pmatrix}$

## Calculating the model predictions {.subsection}

$\text{prediction}_{ij} = \text{expected}_{ij} = \frac{\text{row total}_i \times \text{column total}_j}{n }$

```{r chisq-marginal-totals, echo=TRUE}
n   <- sum(observed)
totExt <- colSums(observed)[1]
totInt  <- colSums(observed)[2]
totDig  <- rowSums(observed)[1]
totLiv <- rowSums(observed)[2]

addmargins(observed)
```

## Prediction under $H_0$ for one cell {.smaller}

- Under $H_0$, lecture type and personality are independent
  - $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B) \qquad P(A \mid B) = P(A)$
- So the share of extroverts is the same for digital and live

```{r chisq-expected-one-cell, echo=TRUE}
pDigital   <- totDig / n    # P(digital), row total / n
pExtrovert <- totExt / n    # P(extrovert), column total / n
pDigital * pExtrovert * n   # predicted number of digital extroverts
```

$\small \text{prediction}_{\text{digital, extrovert}} = \underbrace{\dfrac{`r totDig`}{`r n`}}_{P(\text{digital})} \times \underbrace{\dfrac{`r totExt`}{`r n`}}_{P(\text{extrovert})} \times \underbrace{\;`r n`\;}_{n} = \dfrac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{n} = `r round(totDig / n * totExt / n * n, 2)`$

## Calculating the model {.smaller}

$\text{prediction}_{ij} = \text{expected}_{ij} = \frac{\text{row total}_i \times \text{column total}_j}{n }$

```{r chisq-expected-frequencies, echo=FALSE}
modelPredictions <- matrix( c((totExt  * totDig)  / n,
                              (totExt  * totLiv)  / n,
                              (totInt  * totDig)  / n,
                              (totInt  * totLiv)  / n), 2, 2, 
                            byrow=FALSE, dimnames = dimnames(observed)
)

modelPredictions
```

$\text{prediction}_{ij} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
`r modelPredictions[1,1]` & `r modelPredictions[1,2]` \\
`r modelPredictions[2,1]` & `r modelPredictions[2,2]` \\
\end{pmatrix}$



## Error = Observed - Model {.subsection .smaller}

```{r chisq-error-observed-model, echo=TRUE}
observed

modelPredictions

observed - modelPredictions
```

## Calculating $\chi^2$

$\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(\text{observed}_{ij} - \text{prediction}_{ij})^2}{\text{prediction}_{ij}}$

```{r chisq-test-statistic, echo=TRUE}
# Calculate chi squared
chi.squared <- sum((observed - modelPredictions)^2 / modelPredictions)
chi.squared
```

## Testing for significance {.subsection}

$df = (r - 1) (c - 1)$

```{r chisq-value, echo=FALSE}
df <- 1
visualize_chisq_base(H = chi.squared, df = df, section = "upper", myLimX = c(0, 5))
```

## Checking expected counts {.smaller}

- With 2 $\times$ 2 tables, no expected values should be below 5
- In larger tables, all expected counts should be greater than 1 and no more than 20% less than 5

```{r chisq-expected-check, echo=TRUE}
modelPredictions
```

```{r chisq-assumption-check, echo=FALSE}
dec2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)  # also used by the odds-ratio slides below

minExpected <- min(modelPredictions)
pFisher     <- fisher.test(observed)$p.value
```

- Smallest expected count is `r dec2(minExpected)`, `r if (minExpected >= 5) "so Pearson's $\\chi^2$ holds" else paste0("so use Fisher's exact test ($p$ = ", dec2(pFisher), ")")`
- In JASP via Cells &rarr; Counts &rarr; *Expected*

## Fisher's exact test {.subsection}

Calculates the exact probability of the $\chi^2$ statistic for small samples (at least one cell of the table has an expected count smaller than 5), when the $\chi^2$ approximation does not yet suffice. 

Calculate all possible permutations.

* Expected cell size < 5

## Standardized residuals {.subsection}

$\text{standardized residuals} = \frac{ \text{observed}_{ij} - \text{prediction}_{ij} }{ \sqrt{ \text{prediction}_{ij} } }$

```{r chisq-standardized-residuals, echo=TRUE}
(observed - modelPredictions) / sqrt(modelPredictions)
```

## Effect size {.subsection}

Odds ratio based on the observed values

```{r chisq-effect-size, echo=TRUE}
observed
```

```{r chisq-odds, echo=FALSE}
# Cells by name, so the odds below cannot swap if the table order changes.
digExt <- observed["Digital", "Extrovert"]
digInt <- observed["Digital", "Introvert"]
livExt <- observed["Live", "Extrovert"]
livInt <- observed["Live", "Introvert"]

# Read along the rows (extrovert vs introvert per lecture type) or along the
# columns (digital vs live per personality): both give the same odds ratio.
oddsDig <- digExt / digInt
oddsLiv <- livExt / livInt
oddsExt <- digExt / livExt
oddsInt <- digInt / livInt
oddsRatio <- oddsDig / oddsLiv
```

## Odds visualized {.smaller}

```{r chisq-spine-plot-helper, echo=FALSE}
# Bar widths are the group shares and heights the conditional probabilities, so every
# area is a count. The dashed line is P(outcome) overall, the split under H0; it is a
# weighted average of the two heights, so it sits close to the bigger group.
# Also used by the book example at the end of this file.
spineOR <- function(counts, labels = colnames(counts),
                    cols = palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito")[c(2, 3)]) {
  outcome <- tolower(labels[1])
  group   <- tolower(names(dimnames(counts))[1])
  widths  <- rowSums(counts) / sum(counts)
  pCond   <- counts[, 1] / rowSums(counts)   # P(outcome | group)
  pAll    <- sum(counts[, 1]) / sum(counts)  # P(outcome)
  odds    <- counts[, 1] / counts[, 2]
  x0 <- c(0, cumsum(widths)[-length(widths)])
  x1 <- cumsum(widths)

  # Larger text than the house style: r-stretch shrinks the figure to the space the
  # bullets leave, and the counts must stay readable from the back of the room.
  par(cex = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.0, mar = c(3.6, 4.4, 1.8, 8.5))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1.18), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
       xlab = "", ylab = sprintf("P(%s | %s)", outcome, group))
  title(main = sprintf("OR = %s / %s = %s", dec2(odds[1]), dec2(odds[2]), dec2(odds[1] / odds[2])),
        line = 0.6)
  axis(2, at = seq(0, 1, 0.25), las = 1)
  for (i in seq_along(widths)) {
    if (widths[i] == 0) next  # no answers in this group yet
    rect(x0[i], 0, x1[i], pCond[i], col = cols[1], border = "white", lwd = 3)
    rect(x0[i], pCond[i], x1[i], 1, col = cols[2], border = "white", lwd = 3)
    # Counts mid-tile, nudged off the dashed line when they would sit on it.
    yLow  <- pCond[i] / 2;       if (abs(yLow  - pAll) < 0.07) yLow  <- pAll - 0.1
    yHigh <- (1 + pCond[i]) / 2; if (abs(yHigh - pAll) < 0.07) yHigh <- pAll + 0.1
    text((x0[i] + x1[i]) / 2, yLow,  counts[i, 1], cex = 1.1)
    text((x0[i] + x1[i]) / 2, yHigh, counts[i, 2], cex = 1.1)
    text((x0[i] + x1[i]) / 2, 1.09, paste("odds =", dec2(odds[i])))
    mtext(rownames(counts)[i], side = 1, at = (x0[i] + x1[i]) / 2, line = 0.5, cex = par("cex"))
  }
  segments(0, pAll, 1, pAll, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  mtext(sprintf("P(%s) = %s", outcome, dec2(pAll)), side = 4, at = pAll, las = 1, line = 0.5,
        cex = 0.9 * par("cex"))
  legend("bottom", inset = -0.42, xpd = TRUE, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n",
         fill = cols, border = NA, legend = labels)
}
```

```{r chisq-odds-visualized, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
spineOR(observed)
```

- Bar height is $P(\text{extrovert} \mid \text{lecture})$, bar width the group size
- $\text{odds}_{\text{digital}} = \dfrac{P(\text{extrovert} \mid \text{digital})}{P(\text{introvert} \mid \text{digital})} = \dfrac{`r digExt` / `r totDig`}{`r digInt` / `r totDig`} = \dfrac{`r digExt`}{`r digInt`}$
- Under $H_0$ both bars split at the dashed line, $P(\text{extrovert})$, so $OR = 1$

## Odds {.smaller}

```{r chisq-odds-extrovert-introvert, echo =FALSE}
observed
```

The extrovert/introvert ratio for digital and live audiences:

* $\text{odds}_{\text{digital}} = \frac{\text{extrovert}}{\text{introvert}} = \frac{ `r digExt` }{ `r digInt` } = `r dec2(oddsDig)`$
* $\text{odds}_{\text{live}} = \frac{\text{extrovert}}{\text{introvert}} = \frac{ `r livExt` }{ `r livInt` } = `r dec2(oddsLiv)`$

In the digital responses, there are +- `r dec2(oddsDig)` times as many extroverts as introverts.
In the live responses, there  are +- `r dec2(oddsLiv)` times as many extroverts as introverts.

## Odds ratio

Is the ratio of these odds.

$OR = \dfrac{\text{odds}_{\text{digital}}}{\text{odds}_{\text{live}}} = \dfrac{`r digExt` / `r digInt`}{`r livExt` / `r livInt`} = \dfrac{`r dec2(oddsDig)`}{`r dec2(oddsLiv)`} = `r dec2(oddsRatio)`$

- $OR = 1$ means the same odds in both groups (no association)

## Odds, the other way around {.smaller}

```{r chisq-odds-digital-live, echo =FALSE}
observed
```

Alternatively, we can look at the ratios of digital/live for extroverts and introverts:

* $\text{odds}_{\text{extrovert}} = \frac{\text{digital}}{\text{live}} = \frac{ `r digExt` }{ `r livExt` } = `r dec2(oddsExt)`$
* $\text{odds}_{\text{introvert}} = \frac{\text{digital}}{\text{live}} = \frac{ `r digInt` }{ `r livInt` } = `r dec2(oddsInt)`$

For the extroverts, there are +- `r dec2(oddsExt)` times as many digital viewers as live viewers.
For the introverts, there are +- `r dec2(oddsInt)` times as many digital viewers as live viewers.

## Odds ratio, the other way around {.smaller}

$OR = \dfrac{\text{odds}_{\text{extrovert}}}{\text{odds}_{\text{introvert}}} = \dfrac{`r digExt` / `r livExt`}{`r digInt` / `r livInt`} = \dfrac{`r dec2(oddsExt)`}{`r dec2(oddsInt)`} = `r dec2(oddsExt / oddsInt)`$

$\dfrac{\text{odds}_{\text{digital}}}{\text{odds}_{\text{live}}} = \dfrac{\text{odds}_{\text{extrovert}}}{\text{odds}_{\text{introvert}}} = `r dec2(oddsRatio)`$

- Same OR, whichever way you read the table

For these data, the odds of watching digitally were approximately `r dec2(oddsRatio)` times higher for extroverts than for introverts. The odds ratio also accounts for the scores in both conditions—watching digitally and watching live—by comparing the odds of watching digitally to live viewing across both personality types.

## Odds ratio shortcut

$\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d \\
\end{pmatrix} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
`r digExt` & `r digInt` \\
`r livExt` & `r livInt` \\
\end{pmatrix}$

$OR = \dfrac{a / b}{c / d} = \dfrac{a / c}{b / d} = \dfrac{a \times d}{b \times c} = \dfrac{`r digExt` \times `r livInt`}{`r digInt` \times `r livExt`} = `r dec2((digExt * livInt) / (digInt * livExt))`$

- JASP shows the log odds ratio by default, where $\log(OR) = 0$ means no association

## Book example {.subsection .smaller}

- 200 cats trained to dance, with food or affection as reward
- Training (food or affection, not both)
- Dance (the cat learned to dance or it did not)

```{r chisq-book-counts, echo=TRUE}
cats <- matrix(c(28, 48, 10, 114), nrow = 2,
               dimnames = list(Training = c("Food", "Affection"),
                               Dance    = c("Yes", "No")))
addmargins(cats)
```

## $\chi^2$ and $p$-value {.smaller}

```{r chisq-book-test, echo=TRUE}
# row total x column total / n, for every cell
catsModel <- outer(rowSums(cats), colSums(cats)) / sum(cats)
catsChi   <- sum((cats - catsModel)^2 / catsModel)
catsChi
```

```{r chisq-book-p-value, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
visualize_chisq_base(H = catsChi, df = 1, section = "upper", myLimX = c(0, 40))
```

## Odds visualized {.smaller}

```{r chisq-book-odds-visualized, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
spineOR(cats, labels = c("Danced", "Did not dance"))
```

- Bar height is $P(\text{danced} \mid \text{training})$, bar width the group size
- $\text{odds}_{\text{food}} = \dfrac{P(\text{danced} \mid \text{food})}{P(\text{did not dance} \mid \text{food})} = \dfrac{`r cats["Food", "Yes"]` / `r sum(cats["Food", ])`}{`r cats["Food", "No"]` / `r sum(cats["Food", ])`} = \dfrac{`r cats["Food", "Yes"]`}{`r cats["Food", "No"]`}$
- Under $H_0$ both bars split at the dashed line, $P(\text{danced})$, so $OR = 1$

## Independent predictors {.subsection .smaller}

Accidents in the driving simulator from lecture 17 (alcohol $\times$ speed)

```{r chisq-anova-balanced, echo=FALSE}
# The factorial ANOVA data from lecture 17: 20 participants in every cell.
anovaData <- read.csv(datasetsPath("anova_alcohol_speed_daytime.csv"))
anovaData$alcohol <- factor(anovaData$alcohol, levels = c("none", "some", "much"))
anovaData$speed   <- factor(anovaData$speed,   levels = c("none", "some", "much"))
anovaCounts <- table(anovaData$alcohol, anovaData$speed)
anovaTest   <- chisq.test(anovaCounts)
anovaModel  <- rowSums(anovaCounts)[1] * colSums(anovaCounts)[1] / sum(anovaCounts)
```

```{r chisq-anova-observed, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Alcohol / speed` = levels(anovaData$alcohol),
                        none = as.vector(anovaCounts[, 1]), some = as.vector(anovaCounts[, 2]), much = as.vector(anovaCounts[, 3]),
                        check.names = FALSE), align = "lccc")
```

- $\text{prediction}_{ij} = \frac{`r rowSums(anovaCounts)[1]` \times `r colSums(anovaCounts)[1]`}{`r sum(anovaCounts)`} = `r anovaModel`$ in every cell, same as observed
- Balanced design, so $\chi^2(`r unname(anovaTest$parameter)`) = `r dec2(anovaTest$statistic)`$ ($p = `r dec2(anovaTest$p.value)`$) and alcohol and speed are independent
